title: Ancient Egypt
summary: Ancient Egypt was a society that began around 3150 BCE and lasted until 30 BCE, when it was invaded by the Romans.

paragraphs: Ancient Egypt was a society that began around 3150 BCE and lasted until 30 BCE, when it was invaded by the Romans.
Egypt grew along the Nile River and was at its most powerful in the 2nd millennium BCE. Its land stretched from the Nile Delta to Nubia, a kingdom located mostly in present-day Sudan.
With the water from the Nile, crops were generally good. They were grown after the water from the Nile floods went down.
The Egyptians created a way of writing using hieroglyphics. They also built large temples and tombs, traded with other areas, and had a powerful army.
Their religion had many gods, and its priests were powerful and rich. The Egyptian rulers, called pharaohs, were thought to be close to the gods.

sections.heading: Beginning of farming
paragraphs: People have lived along the Nile for a very long time, according to archaeologists, who study objects left by ancient people. The fertile flood plains of the Nile allowed people to begin farming. By the 10th millennium BCE, the people in Egypt had begun growing cereal grains like wheat and barley.

Because they were farming, people stayed in one place, instead of living a nomadic lifestyle like their ancestors. Because they were settled, society became more complex. That was an important step in the history of human civilization.
This period in Egyptian history is called "predynastic," as it happened before the large dynastic kingdoms were formed.

sections.heading: Development of cultures
paragraphs: By about 5500 BCE, small tribes living in the Nile Valley had developed into a series of cultures. Each had begun farming crops and animals. Each had its own types of pottery and personal items such as combs, bracelets, and beads. In Upper Egypt, the southern part of the country, the Badarian was one of the earliest cultures. It is known for its high-quality pottery, stone tools, and its use of copper. It was followed by the Amratian and the Gerzian cultures.

sections.heading: Periods
paragraphs: The different periods of ancient Egyptian history are:
Predynastic Period (5500 – 3000 BCE)
Early Dynastic Period (1st & 2nd Dynasties, 3000 – 2700 BCE)
Old Kingdom (3rd to 6th Dynasties, 2700 – 2180 BCE)
First Intermediate Period (7th to 11th Dynasties, 2180 – 2050 BCE)
Middle Kingdom (11th to 14th Dynasties, 2080 – 1640 BCE)
Second Intermediate Period (15th to 17th Dynasties, 1640 – 1560 BCE; the Hyksos)
New Kingdom (18th to 20th Dynasties, 1560 – 1070 BCE)
Third Intermediate Period (21st to 25th Dynasties, 1070 – 664 BCE)
Late Period (26th to 31st Dynasties, 664 – 323 BCE; the Persians)
Greco-Roman Egypt (323 – 30 BCE; Ptolemaic to Roman)

During some of the Intermediate periods, the traditional system broke down, and the country was divided or invaded by foreign rulers. During some periods, the Egyptian government was challenged and sometimes overthrown. Still, Egypt's culture and climate were relatively stable compared to those of other parts of the Middle East.

sections.heading: Districts
paragraphs: Ancient Egypt was divided into many different districts, called sepats. The first divisions were created during the Predynastic Period, but they became small city-states that ruled themselves.

When the first pharaoh came to power, the sepats remained and were much like the counties in many countries today. They stayed basically the same for a long time. There were 42 of them, and each was ruled by a governor, chosen by the pharaoh. In later years. the districts were called nomes, and the governor was called a nomarch.

sections.heading: Taxes
paragraphs: Ancient Egypt had many different taxes, but there was no real money and so people paid each other with goods or work. The person who watched the tax collection was a scribe, and all of the tax collectors in Egypt had to state every day how many taxes they had collected.

People paid different taxes based on the work that they did; for example, craftsmen paid in goods, and hunters and fishermen paid with food. Every household in the country paid a labour tax every year by helping with work for the country like mining or working on canals. Many rich Egyptians paid poorer people to do the work for them.

sections.heading: Language
paragraphs: Ancient Egyptian language developed within six time periods.

sections.heading: Archaic Egyptian (before 3000 BCE)
paragraphs: This language has been found on pottery carvings. "Archaic" means very old.

sections.heading: Old Egyptian (3000 BCE to 200 BCE)
paragraphs: This language was used during the Old Kingdom and the First Intermediate Period. It has been found in pyramids and Egyptian tombs. It was the first version of the language to use the plural, which shows that people were discussing more than one object at a time.

sections.heading: Middle Egyptian (2000 BCE to 1300 BCE)
paragraphs: This language is called Classic Egyptian. It has been found all over objects and tombs in Egypt, including Egyptian coffins. Books on science and society were written during this time, and many of the things that are known about religion of the time are written in Classic Egyptian. Even after people stopped speaking this kind of Egyptian, writers still used it when they wrote books.

sections.heading: Late Egyptian (1300 BCE to 700 BCE)
paragraphs: This is the language of the New Kingdom, which was the best time in Egypt's history. Much knowledge was shared during this time, and so many very old books were found that were written in Late Egyptian. Many people believe that this version of the language was much like what the Egyptians spoke.

sections.heading: Demotic and Coptic
paragraphs: Demotic Egyptian was used from around 700 BCE to 400 CE.
Coptic Egyptian was used from around 300 CE to 1700 CE.

sections.heading: Hieroglyphics
paragraphs: Egypt had writing called hieroglyphics, which is one of the two oldest written languages in history. (The other is Sumerian cuneiform.) Hieroglyphic writing dates to c. 3200 BCE and has around 500 symbols. A hieroglyph represents a word, a sound, or a symbol to show what the sign means. The same symbol can serve different purposes in different contexts.
Hieroglyphs on stone monuments and in tombs were for public purposes. It was art and often propaganda.

sections.heading: Hieratic script
paragraphs: Priests used this script for everyday writing on papyrus, wood, or cloth. It was a cursive form of writing, called hieratic, which was quicker and easier to write.
Formal hieroglyphs may be read in rows or columns in either direction but are typically written from right to left. Hieratic was always written from right to left, usually in horizontal rows.

sections.heading: Demotic script
paragraphs: This was the script that ordinary people used and became the main writing style in ancient Egypt. This form of writing and formal hieroglyphs accompanies the Greek text on the Rosetta Stone.

sections.heading: Coptic script
paragraphs: The Coptic script is a modified Greek alphabet. The Coptic language is the last stage of the Egyptian language. (Today, Egyptians speak a dialect of Arabic.)

sections.heading: Literature
paragraphs: Some ancient Egyptian literature has survived to the present day. There are teaching texts such as the Maxims of Ptahhotep, the Instructions of Amenemope, and the Ebers papyrus. The Ebers papyrus is one of the earliest medical texts ever found.
There are also poems and stories.
The story of Sinuhe
An Ancient Egyptian murder mystery written around 1800 BCE.
Ipuwer papyrus
A poem about the ruin of Egyptian society--some think it is about the story in Exodus, a book in the Jewish/Christian Bible.
Westcar papyrus
A series of stories about the Pharaoh Khufu told by his sons.
Papyrus Harris I
The longest papyrus ever found in Egypt.
Story of Wenamun
An ancient adventure story about a priest who goes to collect gifts from a king.

sections.heading: Religion
paragraphs: Religion was very important to Ancient Egyptians. The centre of any Egyptian town was the temple, a building that was used for everything from the town hall to a university, in addition to its religious services.
Because they were so religious, Egyptians created much art depicting many different kinds of divine (holy) creatures, including the pharaoh, who was thought to be a god.

The afterlife was also very important to Egyptians, who are known for mummifying their dead. The mummies are important to scientists today because they provide information about how the Egyptians lived.

sections.heading: Gods and goddesses
paragraphs: All of the gods were important, but some were more important than others.
Isis was the goddess of the sky. Another major god was Ra, who was the god of the sun. The less well-known god of the Nile and crocodiles was named Sobek, which is a rather unusual name.
Bastet was the goddess of cats and so the Ancient Egyptians mummified cats in her honour. She was also the goddess of protection, joy, and families.

sections.heading: Rich soil
paragraphs: The rich fertile soil came from annual floodings of the Nile River. The ancient Egyptians produced plenty of food, which allowed the population to devote more time and resources to cultural, technological, and artistic pursuits. Ancient Egyptian taxes were assessed based on the amount of land a person owned.

Most animals were kept as food. Some animals were kept as pets. All kinds of animals were important to Egypt. Ancient Egyptians understood the animals that they kept: goats, pigs, ducks, cows, and geese.

sections.heading: Farming
paragraphs: Farming in Egypt depended on the cycle of the Nile. The Egyptians recognized three seasons: Akhet (flooding), Peret (planting), and Shemu (harvesting). The flooding season lasted from June to September. The flooding on the river's banks left a layer of mineral-rich silt ideal for growing crops.

After the floodwaters had receded, the growing season lasted from October to February. Farmers plowed and planted seeds in the fields, which were irrigated with ditches and canals. Egypt receives little rainfall and so farmers relied on the Nile to water their crops.p514

From March to May, farmers used sickles to harvest their crops, which were then threshed with a flail to separate the straw from the grain. Winnowing removed the chaff from the grain, which was then ground into flour, brewed to make beer, or stored for later use.p506

sections.heading: Agricultural products
paragraphs: Flax plants were grown for the fibres of their stems. The fibres were split along their length and spun into thread, which was used to weave sheets of linen and to make clothing.
Papyrus grew on the banks of the Nile River and was used to make paper.

Vegetables and fruits were grown in garden plots close to homes and on higher ground. They had to be watered by hand. Vegetables included leeks, garlic, melons, squashes, pulses, lettuce, and other crops. In addition, grapes were made into wine.p577; 630

sections.heading: Medicine
paragraphs: Ancient Egyptians had some advanced medical knowledge for their time. They performed surgery, set broken bones, and even used medicines like honey, breast milk, and gazelle's milk. These had medicinal benefits, but people also thought they kept evil spirits and demons away.

The Edwin Smith papyrus is the world's oldest surviving surgical document, written around 1600 BCE. The text provides detailed descriptions of anatomy and the examination, diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis of 48 types of medical problems.

sections.heading: Pyramids
paragraphs: Ancient Egyptian pyramids are shaped stone masonry structures. They are the best-known pyramid structures and are some of the largest ever buildings. Over 130 pyramids have been discovered in Egypt. Most were built on the western side of the Nile in desert areas. Egyptian pyramids are often contain chambers and passages and were built as the burial places of the Egyptian kings before the start of the Old Kingdom until the end of the Middle Kingdom. Because the Egyptians kept written records, we know about the building of some pyramids.

The Great Pyramid, at Giza, is the largest and most famous pyramid and was built for Pharaoh Khufu. It is over 140 metres tall and took 20 years to build. It is listed as one of the Seven Wonders of the World.
The step pyramid at Saqqara is the earliest pyramid that is still standing today. Built in 2630 BCE, it was a burial place of the Pharaoh Djoser. Its architect was Imhotep.

sections.heading: Other achievements
paragraphs: Engineering was an important activity in Egypt. Engineers measured and surveyed the distance between two points. They designed and made the pyramids, which are nearly perfect geometrically. They also make cement and developed large irrigation networks.
Science was also important. Mathematics was used, and the golden ratio was used in the construction of the pyramids.

Another ability of the Egyptians was glassmaking. Archaeologists have found many pieces of beads, jars, figures, and ornaments in tombs across the nation. In 2005, the remains of an ancient glassmaking factory was found.

sections.heading: Predynastic
paragraphs: 3500 BCE: Senet, a board game, is invented
3500 BCE: Egyptian faience, the world's oldest earthenware, or pottery, is created but is not the same as modern faience pottery

sections.heading: Dynastic
paragraphs: 3300 BCE: Bronze works are first created
3200 BCE: Hieroglyphs are developed
3100 BCE: Decimal system in use
3100 BCE: Mining occurs on Mount Sinai
3100 BCE: Ships are built in Abydos, an Egyptian city
3000 BCE: Trading takes place between Egypt and Palestine
3000 BCE: Copper plumbing in use
3000 BCE: Papyrus, or ancient paper, is first used
3000 BCE: First documented use of medicine
2900 BCE: Perhaps the first steel use in the ancient world
2700 BCE: First surgery performed
2700 BCE: Surveying used by engineers
2700 BCE: Hieroglyphs no longer show only little pictures of words but become based on sounds
2600 BCE: The Great Pyramids of Giza created
2600 BCE: Shipping expeditions occur
2600 BCE: First use of barges
2600 BCE: Pyramid of Djoser created
2600 BCE: Menkaure's Pyramid and the Red Pyramid created
2200 BCE: Government in Egypt collapsed, meaning many different people tried to become pharaoh
1900 BCE: Possible Nile to Red Sea canal created
1650 BCE: The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus is written, which shows knowledge of geometry, arithmetic and algebra
1600 BCE: The Edwin Smith Papyrus is written, which shows knowledge of advanced medical techniques
1550 BCE: The Ebers Medical Papyrus is written, the first document on the topic of tumours
1500 BCE: Glassmaking
1258 BCE: First known peace treaty (Ramesses II)
1160 BCE: The Turin Papyrus is written, the first geologic and topographic map
